subject: psychology
title: Social Influence: Minority Influence & Change
welcome_lead: How does a tiny minority ever overturn the majority? Moscovici has answers.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology minority influence: Moscovici 1969, consistency, commitment, flexibility, social change.
final_note: Minorities change minds by being consistent enough to be heard.

concepts.def: When a small group influences the beliefs of the majority.
Repeating the same message over time and between members.
Showing dedication, often via personal sacrifice — the augmentation principle.
Adapting position without abandoning core view.
Gradual conversion of majority members until a tipping point.
Society remembers the change but forgets the minority who caused it.

walkthroughs.body_html: Moscovici et al. (1969) had two confederates call 36 blue slides 'green'. Consistent confederates produced agreement on 8.42% of trials; inconsistent ones only 1.25%. Minorities work — when they are consistent.

Effective minorities show consistency (synchronic and diachronic), commitment (risking something — augmentation) and flexibility (Nemeth 1986 — rigidity is off-putting). Together these make a majority think harder, driving internalisation.

Social change follows: drawing attention, consistency of position, deeper processing, augmentation through sacrifice, the snowball effect and finally social cryptomnesia. The suffragettes and civil rights movements both fit this template.
